name: Femi Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle home insurance claims at a mutual insurer, the kind that's owned by its members rather than shareholders. Our office is in an old converted mill on the edge of town. Most days it's water damage, burst pipes, storm roofs and the occasional break-in. I read the plumber's or builder's report, check the policy, decide what we cover and write to the customer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle bit, working out whether a stain is a slow leak or a sudden one, because that decides everything. I've been there five years, so I know the policy wording well. What drains me is the decline letters; nobody likes being the one who says no. I use one of the AI chat tools now and then to soften the wording of those letters, and then I rewrite half of it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised; the tools are useful but clumsy. At work I'd joke with Priya, my team leader, that the robot still can't tell a leak from condensation. Online I'd probably not bother posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My job is mostly reading what a plumber wrote about a burst pipe and deciding whether we pay. A bit of software tidying that up won't change my rent. The mutual hasn't made anyone redundant in the five years I've been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the chat tool for letters when I'm stuck. Ada and I would keep putting 300 a month towards a flat deposit, which is the plan anyway. I might go to one of the free lunchtime sessions on the new claim-notes tool, just so I'm not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A small part of me is almost disappointed nothing exciting happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ada do, and how secure is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada's a nurse on a surgical ward at the hospital. Her job isn't going anywhere, and she earns about the same as me. Between us we've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mutual hasn't cut anyone. Would that hold if a few routine tasks moved to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, because we've got more claims than people after last winter's storms. They'd probably just stop paying overtime. That's annoying but it's not frightening.

I wouldn't bother **posting online** about it.

The mutual has made **nobody redundant** in his five years there.
do: Keep using the **chat tool** for tricky decline letters.
Keep saving **300 a month** with Ada towards a flat deposit.
Attend a free **lunchtime session** on the claim-notes tool.
feel: **Relaxed**, and almost a bit **disappointed** nothing exciting happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules, and the people doing the work should help set them. At work I'd be pushing our staff association to get a seat at the table. With friends I'd say it's real, it's not hype this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, reading reports and writing letters is exactly what the software will do. I think the mutual stops hiring clerks, and within three years our team of fifteen is maybe eight. The safer place is out in the field, as a loss adjuster, the person who visits the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priya this month about the trainee loss adjuster scheme, and start the first insurance exam module in spring, around 400 for the fee. I'd get properly good at the AI claim tools, because whoever runs them stays longest. I'd also join the staff association's committee on new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a way that makes me move. It's like seeing a storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes loss adjusting safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You have to go out, stand in the water, smell the damp, talk to an upset family and spot when someone's exaggerating. I'd rather be the person who goes and stands in a flooded kitchen than the person whose screen gets replaced first. Some of it will be done by photos and AI, but not all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you drop the deposit savings to pay for exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask the mutual to pay; they usually fund one module a year. If not, I'd pay it from my own spending money, not the deposit. Ada would kill me.

fieldNote: He spots the **field role** as the hands-on escape route inside his own firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving faster than any law can, and we need a pause or a safety net now. I'd sign every petition going. I'd probably post more in a month than I have in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm done as a clerk by 2028. Two years is shorter than the time it takes to qualify as a loss adjuster. By the time I'd passed the exams, there'd be nobody left to hire me. The field visits might hold until robots arrive around 2031, but that's a three-year window at best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra and push our savings from four months to six. I'd look at hands-on work I could start fast, maybe joining a property repair firm doing the damp surveys I already understand from the claims side. Ada and I would put the flat purchase on hold, because a mortgage with one shaky income is mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winded. Like someone took the plan out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ada that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ada the flat has to wait, and that her ward job is now the one that keeps us. She'd be fine with it, she's practical. I'd be the one who finds it hard, because I wanted to pay my half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned petitions. Do you think they'd change anything in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not on the speed, honestly. But a tax on the firms doing it, paid back to workers, that could happen. I'd vote for that in a heartbeat.

I'd sign **every petition** and post more than I have in years.

Look for hands-on work with a **property repair firm** doing damp surveys.

feel: **Winded**, as if the plan was taken out of his hands.
S2.quote: Two years is shorter than the time it takes to qualify as a loss adjuster. By the time I'd passed the exams, there'd be nobody left to hire me.
fieldNote: The speed kills his **loss adjuster** plan; he notices the timing problem himself.
He'd shift weight to Ada's **nursing job** and finds that hard to accept.
He hopes for a **tax on AI firms** more than for a pause.

steps.text: Cut extras and build savings from four to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if governments start now, so they should start now. At work I'd be telling the younger clerks to get qualified in something. Online I'd share the guides I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me just enough time to get out from behind the desk and into people's damp living rooms, where the robots won't be until 2034. The desk part of my job would go around 2031. So the race is to qualify before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the loss adjuster exams next spring and aim to finish in three years. I'd use the AI tools every day at work so I understand what they can and can't see in a damp photo. We'd still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage works on Ada's pay alone if it has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but okay. It's a deadline, and I'm decent with deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller flat rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent is dead money and Ada's job will still be there. We'd pick a two-bed near the hospital instead of the three-bed we liked. If I end up between jobs, she can cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you around 2034, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe by then the adjuster is the person who checks what the robot found. I'd be 35 and I'd figure the next step out then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, which is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd tell people at work this is the time to retrain without panic. I'd still push for the mutual to share the savings with staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is basically a whole second career. I'd have time to train, buy a flat with my partner and still have savings when the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the loss adjuster qualification over four years, part-time, paid by the mutual. We'd buy the flat in the next two years as planned. I'd keep using AI tools at work and maybe in five years look at a second skill, like building surveying, so I'm not resting on one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit of worry at the back, but it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mutual should share the savings. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our members own it, so if AI saves millions on claims handling, some of that should go to retraining staff, not just lower premiums. I'd raise it at the members' meeting. Our mutual is owned by its members, so I want the members to decide what happens to the people who answer their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd still worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones in the post room, who scan the paper letters. That job is half gone already. Ten years is long for me but short if you're 55.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's faster than any qualification I could get. What would help is the mutual paying for field training now, before anything happens, and some kind of income support while people retrain. Our mutual is supposed to look after its people, so this is the test.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the one writing decline letters while worrying about your own job. I've told a family we won't cover their ceiling, then gone to lunch wondering who'll cover mine. You don't get that in the training manual.

headlineQuote: Our mutual is owned by its members, so I want the members to decide what happens to the people who answer their phones.
portrait: Femi, 27, handles **home insurance claims** at a member-owned mutual and lives with Ada, a nurse.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and moves once a path is proven.
His escape route is becoming a **loss adjuster**, doing field visits robots reach later.
He's calm when nothing changes and **alarmed** only at the two-year pace.
He wants members and staff to **share** in what AI saves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it moves faster than any qualification he could finish.
whatWouldHelp: The mutual paying for **field training** now.
